Leo X. Born Giovanni de' Medici, he reigned as pope from 1513 to 1521. The son of Lorenzo the Magnificent, he was a lavish patron of the arts, representing the peak of Medici influence in the Church. His extravagant lifestyle and extensive spending exhausted the papal treasury.

He was appointed as a cardinal at the exceptionally young age of 13 through his father Lorenzo the Magnificent's political influence. His promotion of the sale of indulgences to fund the rebuilding of St. Peter's Basilica triggered the Protestant Reformation, which he failed to contain. He authorized the aggressive sale of plenary indulgences throughout Germany, notably by the Dominican friar Johann Tetzel, to finance the rebuilding. This directly prompted Martin Luther to post his 95 Theses.

In 1520, Leo issued the papal bull Exsurge Domine, which condemned 41 errors of Martin Luther and threatened him with excommunication. He later carried this out with Decet Romanum Pontificem in 1521. He presided over the closing sessions of the Fifth Lateran Council from 1512 to 1517, which failed to enact the sweeping ecclesiastical reforms that could have prevented the Reformation. In 1516, he negotiated the Concordat of Bologna with King Francis I of France, granting the French monarchy the authority to appoint French bishops and clergy.
